paras: The killing of William Rice was the reported death of Wm. Rice, described as an alleged revenue informer, whose body was rumored in early February 1882 to have been found in Gwinnett County, Georgia, cut nearly in two. The only report, a one-sentence item in the Savannah Morning News, presented the story as a rumor and named no killers, motive or race.

On 9 February 1882 the Savannah Morning News, in its "Georgia Affairs" column of state news briefs, said it was rumored in Covington and Conyers that Rice's body had been found "recently" in Gwinnett County. According to the item, the body was "cut nearly in two." The brief gave no date of death or discovery, no place within the county and no account of how or by whom Rice was killed. It also did not state Rice's race.
No report of an inquest, arrest or trial for Rice's death appears in the coverage.

Rice's death drew a single unheadlined sentence, placed between items on an Atlanta house burglary and a Black mill worker killed by a log train. The Savannah Morning News attributed the story to talk in Covington and Conyers rather than to a correspondent or official, and it offered no comment on the killing. Its one descriptive label for Rice, "an alleged revenue informer," was the only hint the item gave of a possible motive. No other paper's account of the killing was found.

bases: A1 reports only a rumored discovery of the mutilated body of an alleged revenue informer; it names no mob, no killers, no race and no motive, so no episode type beyond an unexplained killing is supported.

A1 reports, as a rumor, that Rice's body was found cut nearly in two, but says nothing about who killed him, how many took part or why, beyond describing him as an alleged revenue informer. Nothing in the coverage shows a group of three or more acting under a pretext of justice, race or tradition.
The only report is one secondhand brief in the Savannah Morning News (A1), which itself presents the story as a rumor current in Covington and Conyers.
